It uses a stochastic SEIRD (susceptible, exposed, infectious, recovered, dead) ensemble model calibrated to 598 cumulative laboratory-confirmed cases as of 8 June 2026, with simulation filtering to retain model runs consistent with that anchor.[291] Under the central scenario (R0 = 1.71), the model projects a median of 990 cumulative confirmed cases by week 12 (24 June 2026; 90% prediction interval 709 to 1,293) and 174 deaths, with cross-border importation into Uganda assessed as nearly certain (94.2%) and into South Sudan as highly probable (69.3%).[292]

Estimate¶

Under the central transmissibility scenario (mean accepted R0 = 1.71), the ensemble projected a median of 648 cumulative confirmed cases by week 10 (8 June 2026; 50% PI 560 to 732), rising to 990 by week 12 (24 June 2026; 50% PI 858 to 1,141 and 90% PI 709 to 1,293), with a projected median of 174 deaths at week 12.[293]

Under the low-transmissibility scenario (mean accepted R0 = 1.42), cumulative confirmed cases reached a median of 870 by week 12 (50% PI 752 to 1,004 and 90% PI 641 to 1,133; 160 deaths) and 3,662 by week 24 (50% PI 2,884 to 4,484 and 90% PI 2,094 to 6,037; 673 deaths).[294]

Under the high-transmissibility scenario (mean accepted R0 = 2.08), confirmed cases reached a median of 1,364 (50% PI 1,154 to 1,579 and 90% PI 975 to 1,807; 202 deaths) by week 12, rising to 66,420 (50% PI 56,560 to 78,937 and 90% PI 41,718 to 95,881; 10,644 deaths) by week 24.[295]

Under the central scenario, week 24 projects a median of 8,210 cumulative confirmed cases (50% PI 6,636 to 10,287 and 90% PI 5,063 to 13,498) and approximately 1,440 deaths if transmission were merely sustained.[296]

The observed confirmed-case trajectory is consistent with the central scenario; the high scenario is retained as an upper-bound contingency should control measures lapse.[297] Importantly, this analysis calibrates exclusively to laboratory-confirmed cases and does not produce a separate “true outbreak size” estimate that exceeds the confirmed count; the reporting fraction was set at 1.0 because laboratory-confirmed cases are, by definition, ascertained, and the earlier suspected-case reporting fraction assumption is no longer required.[10] No detection multiplier is calculated or reported.

Methods¶

Stochastic SEIRD ensemble model: A discrete-time SEIRD framework with daily transitions implemented as binomial draws using standard mass-action incidence, applied to the DRC outbreak (Ituri and Nord Kivu provinces combined). Three transmissibility scenarios span published BDBV estimates: low R0 = 1.42, central R0 = 1.71, and high R0 = 2.08.[298][299][300] Calibration was performed by simulation filtering (approximate rejection sampling, not formal Bayesian inference): replicates were accepted if cumulative laboratory-confirmed cases at day 68 (8 June 2026) fell within ±30% of 598 (range 419 to 777), retaining 400 calibration-passing replicates per scenario.[301] Sensitivity analyses examined travel-while-infectious (5% to 25%), reporting completeness (0.60 to 0.90), and catchment size (250,000 to 500,000).[302]

Daily-hazard spillover model: Importation risk to Uganda, South Sudan, Rwanda, and Burundi was modelled as a daily Poisson hazard driven by calibrated infectious prevalence from the SEIRD model, country-specific cross-border mobility, point-of-entry detection sensitivity from WHO Joint External Evaluation assessments, and travel-while-infectious parameters (Uganda 12%; South Sudan 15%; Rwanda and Burundi 8%), with full equations and parameter values given in an appendix.[303] Importation probability was computed as 1 − exp(cumulative 12-week hazard), yielding the probability of at least one importation for each country.[304]

Assumptions¶

Transmissibility scenarios: Three R0 values (low 1.42, central 1.71, high 2.08) span published BDBV estimates. Response-intensity reductions applied from 15 May 2026 are 20% (low scenario), 25% (central), and 15% (high), reflecting differing assumptions about operational effectiveness.[300][305]

Latent and infectious periods: The latent period is fixed at 9.7 days and the infectious period at 5.0 days, in line with the broader filovirus literature. These are not varied across scenarios.[306]

Case-fatality ratio: Drawn from a uniform distribution (0.15 to 0.25), centred on the observed confirmed-case ratio of approximately 19% (115 of 598 as of 8 June 2026) and consistent with the historical BDBV range.[307]

Ascertainment and reporting fraction: Set at 1.0 for laboratory-confirmed cases on the structural assumption that confirmed cases are fully ascertained by definition. This eliminates the need to estimate an under-detection multiplier but means the model tracks the confirmed trajectory only, not total infections.[10]

Homogeneous mixing and catchment size: The model assumes homogeneous mixing within a single catchment of 350,000 across seven affected health zones, including Ituri and Nord Kivu. Spatial heterogeneity is not captured, acknowledged by the authors as a stated limitation.[308]

Calibration tolerance: Simulation filtering accepts replicates if cumulative confirmed cases at day 68 fall within ±30% of 598 (range 419 to 777). The ±30% tolerance was chosen pragmatically given residual data uncertainty, and is not derived from formal inference.[309][310]

Cross-border mobility and travel-while-infectious parameters: The spillover model uses country-specific travel-while-infectious parameters (Uganda 12%; South Sudan 15%; Rwanda and Burundi 8%) alongside WHO Joint External Evaluation-based detection sensitivity. The authors acknowledge these parameters were not empirically derived for this outbreak and represent the principal sources of uncertainty in spillover projections.[311][312]

No vaccination compartment: No vaccinated compartment was included, reflecting the absence of a licensed BDBV-specific vaccine.[313]

Model type: These projections are described by the authors as exploratory preparedness-oriented estimates derived from a stochastic scenario-based modelling framework, rather than predictions generated from formally fitted epidemiological models using comprehensive parameter estimation and identifiability analyses.[314]

Limitations¶

Homogeneous mixing and absent spatial structure: The model oversimplifies spatial heterogeneity across health zones, does not separately model healthcare-worker transmission, and applies response intensity uniformly rather than varying it by place, time, access, or community acceptance.[20]

Single-point calibration anchor: The model is anchored on a single recent confirmed-case datum (598 on 8 June 2026), making the fit sensitive to that anchor.[20]

Simulation filtering is not formal inference: Calibration by approximate rejection sampling is acknowledged as not constituting formal Bayesian inference, and informal cross-border mobility estimates are described as imprecise.[20]

Uniform and static response intensity: The response-intensity factor was applied uniformly from 15 May, but real-world response effectiveness varies by place, time, access, and community acceptance. Live mobility data and behavioural adaptation were not incorporated.[315]

Surveillance dynamics and residual confounding: The post-declaration case-finding surge probably contributed to rapid apparent growth between 15 and 19 May; the analysis addressed this by lowering the reporting fraction and widening the calibration window, but residual confounding between transmission intensity and surveillance intensity remains.[316]

Early-phase data quality: Calibration initially relied on early-phase surveillance counts from the first weekly WHO External Situation Report, where the suspected-case total was only partially resolved into laboratory-confirmed cases and death counts reflected surveillance signals rather than confirmed mortality alone. Misclassification, delayed laboratory throughput, and ongoing active case finding could each shift the calibration anchor in either direction. The projections are therefore interpreted as an early situational assessment rather than a definitive forecast.[317]

Need for iterative recalibration: The projections require iterative recalibration as new data emerge.[318]

Data sources¶

Primary outbreak data: Case data were taken from WHO AFRO External Situation Reports and the WHO AFRO internal tracker through 8 June 2026. The laboratory-confirmed case series used as the primary calibration metric ran from 33 cases on 18 May 2026 to 105 on 24 May 2026 and 598 on 8 June 2026.[319] WHO External Situation Report 01 (as of 18 May 2026) documented 528 cumulative suspected cases, 132 deaths, and 35 laboratory-confirmed cases across DRC and Uganda.[320] Uganda’s confirmed case count of 19 as of 4 June 2026 (including five healthcare-worker infections and two deaths) is used to validate the spillover model output.[321]

Auxiliary data: Transmissibility scenario ranges were chosen to span published BDBV estimates from the 2007 Uganda and 2012 DRC outbreaks. The latent period was fixed at 9.7 days and the infectious period at 5.0 days, in line with the broader filovirus literature. The CFR was drawn from a uniform distribution (0.15 to 0.25), centred on the observed confirmed-case ratio of approximately 19% (115 of 598 as of 8 June 2026) and consistent with the historical BDBV range.[322] Point-of-entry detection sensitivity values for the spillover model were drawn from WHO Joint External Evaluation assessments; travel-while-infectious parameters (Uganda 12%; South Sudan 15%; Rwanda and Burundi 8%) were applied country-specifically.[311] Published reproduction number estimates from previous BDBV outbreaks in Uganda (2007) and DRC (2012), ranging from 1.2 to 2.6, informed scenario boundaries.[323]

McCabe et al. (27 May 2026)
Estimation of the Ebola outbreak size in the Democratic Republic of the Congo¶

Read the analysis

Overview¶

This analysis produces early estimates of the epidemic size in the Democratic Republic of the Congo as of May 27, 2026, using two independent, scenario-based methods applied under plausible assumptions about surveillance, severity, and epidemic growth.[324] The first method back-calculates cases from reported deaths using historical case fatality ratios and onset-to-death delays; the second estimates outbreak size from confirmed imported cases in Uganda combined with cross-border travel volumes. The two methods yield broadly consistent results, suggesting that approximately 280–2,520 cases of Bundibugyo virus disease may have occurred in DRC as of May 27, 2026.[4]

Estimate¶

Back-calculation from deaths: Assuming 30% of suspected and confirmed deaths are due to Ebola, a CFR of 33%, and a doubling time of 10 days, the mean estimated outbreak size is 451 cases (95% CI 396–511) as of May 27, 2026.[325] The estimated outbreak size increases with assumptions of a higher proportion of deaths due to Ebola, a lower CFR, and faster epidemic growth.[15] The full scenario range for this method is 306–2,521 cases.[4]

Travel-based back-calculation: Assuming Ituri Province as the source population and a doubling time of 10 days, the mean estimated outbreak size is 945 cases (95% CI 196–2,274).[326] The full scenario range for this method is 282–1,345 cases.[4]

Cross-method synthesis: Together, the two methods suggest that approximately 280–2,520 cases of Bundibugyo virus disease might have occurred in DRC as of May 27, 2026, with considerable uncertainty around these estimates.[4]

Methods¶

Back-calculation from deaths: This method links reported suspected and confirmed deaths — assuming a proportion are attributable to Ebola — with estimates of the case fatality ratio (33%, 95% CI 26–40%) and the distribution of time from symptom onset to death (gamma distribution, mean 11.37 days, SD 5.41) derived from previous Bundibugyo virus outbreaks.[327] The method further assumes exponential epidemic growth after a single zoonotic spillover event.[328] It applies to DRC, with transmission assumed concentrated in Ituri and Nord Kivu. Sensitivity analyses vary the epidemic growth rate (main scenario: 10-day doubling time; sensitivity 1: 7-day doubling time; sensitivity 2: 14-day doubling time) and the proportion of suspected and confirmed deaths attributable to Ebola (main scenario: 30%; an additional analysis assumes 100%).[329]

Travel-based back-calculation (geographical spread model): This method extends the approach described by Imai and colleagues (2020) during the COVID-19 pandemic, combining information on three confirmed imported BVD cases reported in Uganda as of May 27, 2026, estimates of daily international travel volumes from Ituri and Nord Kivu provinces to Uganda, assumptions about epidemic doubling time, and the presumption that all cases in symptomatic travellers will be detected at the time of recovery or death.[330] The main analysis uses Ituri Province as the source population (n=4,392,200); a sensitivity run expands this to include Nord Kivu (combined n=12,593,600).[331] An additional sensitivity analysis assumes only one imported case rather than three.[332]

Assumptions¶

Proportion of deaths attributable to Ebola: The percentage of deaths attributable to Ebola is assumed to lie between 30% and 100%.[333] The main scenario uses 30%, with 100% explored in a supplementary analysis. This is a key driver: the estimated outbreak size increases with assumptions of a higher proportion of deaths due to Ebola.[15]

CFR and onset-to-death distribution: The CFR is fixed at 33% (95% CI 26–40%) and the onset-to-death distribution is a gamma with mean 11.37 days and SD 5.41, both derived from previous Bundibugyo virus outbreaks.[327] The assumption that these parameters are consistent with those from prior outbreaks carries substantial uncertainty.[333]

Epidemic growth rate: The current epidemic growth rate is assumed to correspond to a doubling time of between 7 and 14 days, loosely based on early genomic analyses.[333] The main scenario uses a 10-day doubling time; sensitivity analyses use 7- and 14-day doubling times.

Single zoonotic spillover and exponential growth: The model assumes exponential epidemic growth after a single zoonotic spillover event.[328] No spatial structure is modelled.

Geographic concentration of transmission: Transmission is assumed to be largely concentrated in Ituri and Nord Kivu provinces.[333]

Travel volumes and traveller detection: The geographical spread model presumes that all cases in symptomatic travellers will be detected at the time of recovery or death.[334] The scale and patterns of population movement from these provinces to Uganda are assumed to be accurately captured in point-of-entry data.[333]

Medical-care-seeking bias in imported cases: At least two of the three imported cases reportedly traveled to Uganda specifically to seek medical care, which the authors flag as a reason to interpret the sensitivity analysis expanding the source population to Nord Kivu with caution.[335]

Limitations¶

Early-stage analysis under scarce data: The analysis is an early assessment, primarily conducted to inform operational planning, and the estimates may change as more data and information become available.[336]

Uncertain assumptions with substantial individual uncertainty: Each of the key assumptions — including the geographic concentration of transmission, the accuracy of travel flow data, the proportion of deaths attributable to Ebola, the applicability of historical CFR and onset-to-death parameters, and the epidemic doubling time — carries substantial uncertainty that may influence the estimates.[13]

Wide confidence intervals from small numerators: The travel-based method rests on only three observed imported cases, producing a mean estimate of 945 cases with a 95% CI of 196–2,274[326] — a very wide interval reflecting the small numerator.

Incomplete and evolving case data: Testing expanded rapidly for routine and retrospective assessment of suspected cases, deaths are harder to retrospectively assess with investigations ongoing, and suspected cases and deaths are no longer reported in recent situation reports[337] — all of which limit the reliability of the input death counts.

Medical-care-seeking bias in exported cases: The findings from the sensitivity analysis expanding the source population should be interpreted with caution, as at least two of the three imported cases reportedly travelled to Uganda specifically to seek medical care[335], making them non-representative of the broader travelling population.

Data sources¶

Primary outbreak data: The analysis uses 1,031 suspected or confirmed cases and 240 suspected or confirmed deaths reported from 14 health zones across Ituri, Nord Kivu, and Sud Kivu as of May 27, 2026.[5] It also uses 3 confirmed imported cases in Uganda from Ituri as of May 27, 2026 (with a total of 16 Uganda cases confirmed as of June 4, 2026).[338]

Auxiliary data: The CFR (33%, 95% CI 26–40%) and the onset-to-death distribution (gamma, mean 11.37 days, SD 5.41) are derived from previous Bundibugyo virus outbreaks.[327] Daily international travel volume estimates from Ituri and Nord Kivu to Uganda are used as inputs to the geographical spread model.[334] The source population sizes are fixed values: Ituri Province at 4,392,200 and Ituri plus Nord Kivu at 12,593,600.[331] The geographical spread method itself extends the analytical framework of Imai and colleagues (2020), developed during the COVID-19 pandemic.[339]

Mooring et al. (24 May 2026)
Modeled Scenario Projections for the Ebola Disease Outbreak Caused by Bundibugyo Virus, 2026¶

Read the analysis

Overview¶

This CDC analysis uses a branching process transmission model to project the future trajectory of the 2026 BVD outbreak over a 90-day horizon, estimating how large the outbreak could become under different assumptions about the current number of deaths and different levels of patient isolation. The model was calibrated to three putative cumulative death counts and projected for four possible intervention scenarios ranging from poor (20%) to extremely high (95%) levels of isolation and treatment of symptomatic persons.[340] The central finding is that without high levels of patient isolation, the outbreak is likely to grow very large: with poor isolation levels of patients with BVD (20%) and no other interventions, the likelihood of an outbreak that exceeds 20,000 cases within 3 months is 65%.[341]

Estimate¶

This analysis produces forward projections rather than a current true case count estimate; it does not provide a detection multiplier or a point estimate of true cases at the data cutoff. The projections are expressed as probabilities of exceeding case or death thresholds within 90 days of May 24, 2026, under three death-calibration scenarios and four isolation scenarios.

Under the 50 deaths calibration: assuming 20% of infected persons were successfully isolated beginning May 24, 2026, projections showed ≥20,000 cumulative cases in 65% of simulations, ≥10,000 cumulative cases in 85% of simulations, and ≥4,000 cumulative deaths in 69% of simulations.[342] At 70% isolation, 94% of simulations projected <10,000 cases and only 1% projected ≥20,000 cases; similarly, 90% of simulations projected <2,000 deaths and only 3% projected ≥4,000 deaths.[343]

Under the 100 deaths calibration: very large outbreaks were likely in the scenario in which only 20% of patients were isolated (76% of simulations projected ≥20,000 cases and 87% projected ≥4,000 deaths).[344] In the scenario in which 70% of infected persons were isolated, 73% of simulations projected <2,000 cumulative deaths by August 22, 2026, and 10% projected ≥4,000 deaths.[345]

Under the 200 deaths calibration: even with 70% of infected persons isolated, 42% of simulations projected ≥10,000 cases by August 22, 2026.[346]

The median basic reproductive number R₀ = 2.51 (IQI = 2.27−2.82) in the main analysis calibrated to 50 deaths.[347]

Methods¶

Branching process model: A branching process model with the capacity to model transmission-reducing nonpharmaceutical interventions was calibrated to three putative cumulative death counts and projected for four possible intervention scenarios.[340] Each simulated outbreak was initialized with one infected person representing a zoonotic spillover event; this person infected a randomly generated number of additional persons based on assumptions about the basic reproductive number (R₀), and any infected persons were added to the simulation at times selected according to the distribution of intervals from one infection to the next, in turn able to cause further infections.[348] The model was adapted from one applied to previous viral hemorrhagic fever outbreaks, including a Marburg virus disease outbreak in Ethiopia in 2025.[349]

Calibration to cumulative deaths: The model was calibrated to three different numbers of cumulative deaths (50, 100, and 200) to account for uncertainty in the current number of deaths caused by BVD; a simulated outbreak was considered compatible with the real-world outbreak if it reached the assumed number of cumulative deaths by May 24, 2026, and if the first death occurred on or before April 24, 2026. Outbreaks were simulated until 500 simulations met these criteria.[350] Assumptions for the cumulative number of BVD deaths as of May 24, 2026, were based on publicly available situation reports from DRC.[351]

Scenario projections: Four intervention scenarios were assessed for each calibration, each implementing a different level of isolation (i.e., percentage of symptomatic infected persons detected, isolated, and treated: 20% [poor], 50% [moderate], 70% [high], and 95% [extremely high]).[352] Each simulation reported the cumulative number of cases and cumulative number of deaths from the date of spillover until August 22, which would be 90 days after interventions began.[353] The analysis applies to the DRC outbreak broadly, without explicit subnational stratification.

Assumptions¶

Zoonotic seed and single-origin start: Each simulated outbreak was initialized with one infected person, who represented the person first infected from a zoonotic source (a spillover event).[354] This structural assumption of a single spillover constrains inferences about outbreak onset timing.

Basic reproductive number (R₀): Each simulated infected person infected a randomly generated number of additional persons based on assumptions about R₀, the average number of persons in a susceptible population infected by an infected person.[355] The median R₀ = 2.51 (IQI = 2.27−2.82) in the main analysis calibrated to 50 deaths.[347] Basic reproductive number estimates for Ebola disease vary widely across outbreaks, and the true value of R₀ for this outbreak might be higher or lower than the values used in this analysis.[356] The analysis did not provide evidence that R₀ for this outbreak is unusually large.[357]

Delay distributions: Intervals from infection to symptom onset, symptom onset to death, and symptom onset to recovery were held constant for all infections within each simulated outbreak but varied among simulated outbreaks.[358] The specific distributional forms and parameter values are not detailed in this document beyond that they were drawn from published Ebola estimates.

Cumulative deaths at calibration date: The model was calibrated to three different numbers of cumulative deaths (50, 100, and 200) to account for uncertainty in the current number of deaths caused by BVD.[359] The true number of BVD deaths that occurred through May 24, 2026, is unknown; some deaths from BVD might not have been confirmed, and it is possible that other deaths might have been incorrectly attributed to BVD.[360]

Isolation intervention mechanics: On the intervention start date, the designated percentage of symptomatic persons was selected to begin isolating, with an average delay of 2 days until isolation and treatment; the same percentage of persons who later developed signs or symptoms was selected to begin isolating with an average delay of 2 days from symptom onset. Simulated persons in isolation were prevented from causing any onward transmission, and the model implicitly assumed that isolated persons who died were safely buried.[361]

No behavioral change: Changes in behavior that reduce risk for infection (e.g., avoiding contact with ill persons) were not included in the model and might help limit outbreak size.[362]

No immunity accumulation: The model did not account for transmission reductions attributable to an increase in the proportion of the population with infection-induced immunity. Given the population size of the communities where this outbreak is occurring, this limitation is unlikely to affect the validity of the projections over the time span and numerical ranges of cases presented in this analysis; however, the model could project unrealistically large outbreaks if applied to longer periods.[363]

No relapses: The model did not include infection relapses after recovery, which is unlikely to affect this analysis, but relapses could be important drivers of the course of the epidemic over a longer period.[364]

Limitations¶

Uncertainty in current death counts: The true number of BVD deaths that occurred through May 24, 2026, is unknown. Some deaths from BVD might not have been confirmed; similarly, it is possible that other deaths might have been incorrectly attributed to BVD.[360] The analysis addresses this by calibrating to three different death counts (50, 100, 200) rather than resolving the uncertainty.

R₀ uncertainty: Basic reproductive number estimates for Ebola disease vary widely across outbreaks, and the true value of R₀ for this outbreak might be higher or lower than the values used in this analysis. High-quality data on changes in the number of cases and deaths over time are essential to more precisely estimate R₀.[365]

Behavioral change not modelled: Changes in behavior that reduce risk for infection (e.g., avoiding contact with ill persons) were not included in the model and might help limit outbreak size.[362]

No immunity depletion: The model did not account for transmission reductions attributable to an increase in the proportion of the population with infection-induced immunity, which is unlikely to affect projections over the time span and numerical ranges presented but could cause the model to project unrealistically large outbreaks if applied to longer periods.[363]

No relapses: The model did not include infection relapses after recovery, which is unlikely to affect this analysis, but relapses could be important drivers of the course of the epidemic over a longer period.[364]

Data sources¶

Primary outbreak data: Assumptions for the cumulative number of BVD deaths as of May 24, 2026, were based on publicly available situation reports from DRC.[351] The DRC national public health institute reported 10 confirmed deaths and 223 suspected deaths as of May 24, 2026.[366] A subsequent report with data as of June 2, 2026, reported a cumulative total of 62 confirmed deaths in DRC.[367] These reports drove the three calibration targets (50, 100, and 200 deaths), used to bracket uncertainty about true death counts.

Auxiliary data (parameters from prior outbreaks): Assumptions about parameters were based on published estimates from previous Ebola outbreaks; estimates specific to BVD were used when available.[368] The analysis does not specify by name which published studies or datasets were used for delay distributions or other parameters. No travel data, demographic data, or line list data from the current outbreak are mentioned as inputs.

References¶

Methods overview

These pages are produced by a semi-automated evidence-synthesis pipeline that pairs AI models with human review at each major checkpoint: one model reads each source analysis on its own and grounds every extracted claim in a verbatim quoted passage; a second model takes the resulting structured comparison as input, and drafts the narrative. Human analysts then review and edit the output to ensure accuracy and completeness prior to publishing.

Identifying analyses. Analyses are identified through continuous monitoring of preprint servers, peer-reviewed publications, and grey literature. An analysis is included if it directly addresses the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak and provides a quantitative estimate relevant to a given topic (e.g., outbreak size, risk of spread). Each included source is logged, and if the authors later release an updated version, the newer version supersedes the earlier one.

Preparing the source text. Each source text, regardless of source type (e.g., PDF, HTML), is converted to Markdown. A human analyst then curates the converted file and removes sections that carry no evidentiary content, such as references, acknowledgments, author contributions, affiliations, and declarations of interest, to keep extraction focused and reduce the number of input tokens used.

Extracting structured evidence. The curated text is split into individually citeable units, one per sentence, and passed to Claude Sonnet 5-5. For each of a fixed set of dimensions (e.g., estimates, methods, limitations), the model answers from that one source alone and must ground every factual claim in a verbatim span of its text.

Synthesizing the narrative. OpenAI’s GPT-5.5 model reads the dimensions extracted for each analysis and synthesizes the information, covering the state of the evidence, how the estimates compare and why they diverge, the key uncertainties and assumptions shared across analyses, what would most reduce that uncertainty, and what it implies for the response.

Human review and publication. Human analysts edit the draft for accuracy, completeness, and tone prior to publishing.

Limitations. This pipeline surfaces only publicly available analyses; works that have not been made public are not captured.
